# Guṇajātaka (Ja 157)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Favors

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Guṇajātaka* (Ja 157), alternatively referred to in traditional indices and scholarship as the *Sīhajātaka* or *Siha-jātaka*, is a birth story in the canonical Pali *Jātaka* collection [Fausböll 1897; Lamotte 1973; SuttaCentral]. According to its commentary's nidāna, the Buddha related the discourse while residing at Jetavana in connection with Venerable Ānanda receiving an offering of a thousand robes after preaching to the ladies of the court in the palace of the king of Kosala [SuttaCentral]. The core narrative concerns a lion who displays affection (*sineha*) toward a jackal that had previously saved his life [Collins 2016]. At the conclusion of the story (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the jackal was Ānanda in a previous existence, while the lion was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1879].

Text-reuse analysis recorded by DharmaNexus indicates five matching passages internally shared with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Dutiyo bhāgo*), the longest segment running between §2.1–2.5 and §136_1–136_2 [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan traditions [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. In his study of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Étienne Lamotte observes that an avadāna of a *Siṃhajātaka* cited in the *Mahākarmavibhaṅga* corresponds to the *Siṃhacandrabuddhajātaka* (Taishō 176) rather than this Pali Jātaka [Lamotte 1973].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§2.1–2.5 ↔ §136_1–136_2)
